title: Did American slavery really end in 1865?
subject: histoire
description: The Thirteenth Amendment abolished slavery in the United States in 1865, except as punishment for a crime. The South seized on that exception at once to force freed Black Americans back into unpaid labor.
author: nathan-hewitt

hero.hook: In 1865, the American Constitution abolished slavery "except as a punishment for crime": all the South had to do was manufacture criminals.

blocks.text: Slavery had been part of the United States since the country was born. Little by little, economic development and new moral convictions wore it down: by the **mid-19th century**, most Northern states had abolished it. The Southern states, however, still depended on slave labor. In **1861**, they left the Union to preserve it: the [[American Civil War]] had begun.

Union troops fought to regain control of the South and end slavery for good. After their victory, it was officially abolished by an amendment to the Constitution. But the text contained one exception, a single one, that would allow slavery to continue under another name, long after everyone believed it was gone.

sections.title: The Civil War and the Emancipation Proclamation

blocks.text: The Civil War had one cause above all: slavery. The farms and plantations that powered the Southern economy ran on slave labor. When [[Abraham Lincoln]] was elected president, the South feared he would outlaw it. Its states seceded, and war broke out in **1861**.

blocks.caption: Lincoln writes the Emancipation Proclamation in his cluttered study: lithograph after the painting by David Gilmour Blythe, 1863.

blocks.text: The war went the Union's way, and its soldiers freed slaves as they pushed into Confederate territory. In **1863**, Lincoln issued the [[Emancipation Proclamation]]: all slaves still held in Confederate territory were to be free. Those who reached Union lines were promised their freedom and could even enlist in its army.

Yet the Proclamation did not end all slavery. Some states that had stayed loyal to the Union still allowed it. And the text did not apply to Confederate regions already occupied by Northern troops, such as **Tennessee**. To finish the job, the Constitution itself had to change.

sections.title: The Thirteenth Amendment and its exception

blocks.text: Lincoln therefore wanted total abolition, written into the Constitution. The [[Thirteenth Amendment]], outlawing slavery, was approved by the Senate in **April 1864**, then rejected by the House of Representatives. To win the House over, Lincoln made it a central promise of his campaign in the election of 1864, which he won in a landslide. Faced with that popular support, the House approved the amendment a few months later.

blocks.caption: The congressional resolution proposing the Thirteenth Amendment, signed by Lincoln in 1865: it contains the clause "except as a punishment for crime."

blocks.text: The Thirteenth Amendment was fully ratified after the war, on **December 6**, 1865. Every slave in the United States was free, and no one could ever be enslaved again. But one exception was written into the text: slavery and involuntary servitude remained allowed as **punishment for a crime**.

This loophole allowed slavery to continue as long as the victim counted as a criminal. The Southern states seized on it immediately. They passed the [[Black Codes]], a set of laws designed to turn Black Americans into offenders and force them back into the fields and plantations.

Living without a job or a permanent home, known as [[vagrancy]], became a crime. And most freed slaves, with no work and no roof, fit that definition as soon as they left slavery. Countless free Black people were arrested for vagrancy and sentenced to **forced labor**.

blocks.caption: Convicts leased out in Florida to harvest timber, chained together: photograph by the Detroit Publishing Co., around 1903.

blocks.text: To escape forced labor, Black Southerners had to find work at any price. White landowners exploited their desperation to impose abusive contracts, and leaving a contract was illegal: they were trapped. In a book that won the **Pulitzer Prize**, Douglas Blackmon summed up the system in one phrase: "slavery by another name."

sections.title: From the Black Codes to today's prisons

blocks.text: These abuses were predictable, and they outraged many in the North. In **1866**, to fight the Black Codes, Congress passed the [[Fourteenth Amendment]], which guarantees every American equal protection under the law. But the South found other loopholes, and thousands of Black people were forced into unfree labor for the state. These practices survived under the [[Jim Crow laws]], the South's legal segregation, into the **20th century**.

According to the American legal scholar Michelle Alexander, these laws have an heir: the prison system. Prisoners, among whom Black Americans are heavily overrepresented, are often made to do underpaid work while serving their sentences. For her, as for many others, America thus carries on the legacy of slavery through its prisons.

events.title: The Fourteenth Amendment
events.detail: Congress answers the Black Codes with equal protection under the law.

blocks.text: The Thirteenth Amendment abolished slavery in 1865 but allowed it as punishment for a crime, and the South immediately turned freed Black Americans into convicts to force them back to work, a system whose trace American prisons still bear.
